title: Al-Qawiyy, the Strong
tomorrow: strength runs out. what kind doesn't?

lines: NEW TOWN, NOTHING IN YOUR POCKETS.
A WELL, AND A SHOVING CROWD.
cards: New town. No job, no friends, no idea where you'll sleep tonight. And the one thing you need, water, has a crowd around it that won't let anyone weak get near.
That's where Moses is. He has fled Egypt with nothing. He reaches a well in Midian, and the shepherds are shoving their flocks to the front.
Off to one side, two young women hold their sheep back and wait. He asks why. They tell him they can't water until the shepherds are done, and their father is a very old man.
So Moses walks into the crowd.

teach.h: HE WATERS, THEN SITS IN THE SHADE.
teach.b: He waters their flock for them. Then he does something the hero of a movie never does.

teach.h: I AM NEEDY OF WHATEVER GOOD.
teach.b: He walks off into the shade, sits down, and says, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest down for me."
A minute after the strongest moment in the scene, the strong man says out loud that he's empty.
Later one of the women tells her father: "O my father! Hire him! For the best (man) that thou canst hire is the strong, the trustworthy." She saw both, the arms at the well and the man in the shade.
Today's Name is Al-Qawiyy, the Strong.
Muslims keep a short phrase for heavy days that hands strength back to where it comes from: la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah, there is no power and no strength except with Allah.
The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, called it a treasure from the treasures of Paradise. Notice what the phrase doesn't say. It doesn't say you're weak, or that you should sit still.
It says the strength was lent. And here's the detail worth telling a friend tonight: in this story, the prayer for help comes after the strong act, not instead of it.

how: Muslims often say la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah when facing something heavy, and call on Allah as Al-Qawiyy, the Strong, in personal du'a.

o: the Strong, whose strength never has to be lent
the Patient, who waits for the right moment
the Mighty, who defeats every enemy in battle

games.q: who did what at the well — tap the pairs.
p: watered, then sat in the shade

s: la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah means you're too weak to try
Moses still hauled the water. the phrase says the strength was lent, not that you sit still.
one of the women called Moses strong and trustworthy
"the best (man) that thou canst hire is the strong, the trustworthy."
Moses prayed for help before he went into the crowd
he watered the flock first, then turned to the shade and said: I am needy.

games.q: your friend carried the whole group project. afterward she tells you, quietly, that she's running on empty. what does the well in Midian say about her?
o: a real leader keeps that to herself until it's over.
she did the strong thing, and saying she's empty is part of it.
she should have asked for help instead of doing the work.
games.why: Moses watered the flock, then said "I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest." the story keeps both: the strong act and the honest ask.

practice: Bring to mind one thing this week that feels heavier than you are: a test, a talk you're dreading, someone you're caring for.

On each slow out-breath, say quietly la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah, or in English, no strength except with God. If the words aren't yours, let the breath itself do the saying, and let the weight be shared for two minutes.

wordCard.voice: Al-Qawiyy. The Strong: the Name behind the arms at the well, and behind the man in the shade who asked.

orig.note: Arabic: the Strong. it shares a root with quwwa, the strength in la hawla wa la quwwata.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: his strength, lent to you for the bucket, the hill and the hard talk. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Qur'an 28:22–25 (Moses at the well of Midian)

sources.q: My Lord! I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest down for me.
O my father! Hire him! For the best (man) that thou canst hire is the strong, the trustworthy.
